stories.headline: Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions in 'National Interests,' Drawing Bipartisan Criticism
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia that were due to take effect under a sweeping sanctions package he signed into law last month. The legislation, dedicated posthumously to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was meant to pressure the Kremlin and included hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian energy. Trump told Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Reporting indicates the measures complicated the administration's effort to lower diesel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. The waiver follows a surprise deal last week allowing Russia to sell diesel internationally, a move Republicans have condemned as loudly as Democrats. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, called the decision "beyond irresponsible," and several other GOP lawmakers also criticized it.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said things were "difficult" without the support of Graham, and reported that Russia had targeted Ukraine's energy sector with more than 320 drones, missiles and munitions. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC the United States risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping end it.

The administration has framed the step as a way to ease energy prices for American consumers. Critics in both parties argue it relaxes pressure on Moscow while the war continues. Congress could respond in the coming days as lawmakers weigh whether to challenge the waiver.

stories.headline: Fact Check: Trump's Midterm Rally Claims on Immigration Costs and Leakers
stories.summary:
As President Trump campaigns in battleground states ahead of the midterms, PBS NewsHour's Liz Landers fact-checked several claims from his recent rallies. At an Ohio rally, Trump said Somali immigrants drive up taxes, health care, insurance and childcare costs and "cheat on everything."

Landers noted that the Congressional Budget Office projects the immigration surge that began in 2024 will add $1.2 trillion to federal revenue over ten years, with the annual increase reaching $164 billion by 2034. Undocumented immigrants are not eligible for Medicaid, and lawfully present immigrants generally face a five-year wait. KFF has found immigrants are not more likely than U.S.-born citizens to report using government assistance for food, housing or health care.

At an Arizona rally, Trump said "leakers should be shot," apparently referring to recent leaks about U.S. strikes on Iran. Landers noted most leaks are prosecuted under the Espionage Act of 1917, which carries severe penalties but is not typically applied as a death-penalty statute for leaking.

Trump's supporters view his rally rhetoric as a forceful articulation of concerns about immigration and national security, and Republicans see the rallies as key to energizing the base. Critics, including many Democrats, say the claims are inaccurate and inflammatory. Eleven outlets across the political spectrum covered the remarks and the fact-checking.

stories.headline: Community Leaders Link Foiled Hindu Temple Attack in Illinois to Surge in Online Hate
stories.summary:
Authorities arrested 19-year-old Alexandros Paporakis on Wednesday in connection with a thwarted mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois. Officials said he drove to the temple Sunday afternoon with a rifle and body armor and waited in the parking lot for several minutes before leaving after his weapon jammed. Thousands were inside observing the first day of Navaratri.

Paporakis was arrested near his home in Palatine after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his stated plan to "kill Indian people." Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was inside the temple with his parents, said the community was shaken. At a Friday news conference in Chicago, he and other leaders called for the attempted attack to be investigated as a hate crime.

Community advocates said anti-Hindu and anti-Indian rhetoric has grown online. Pushpita Prasad of the Coalition of Hindus of North America warned that "sooner or later, all that online hate is going to migrate to the real world." Recent incidents include bricks thrown at a temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, on Oct. 3, and a June 2025 shooting at a temple in Spanish Fork, Utah.

Leaders are calling for an organized community response to prevent hate and extremism targeting all communities.

stories.headline: Tesla Unveils Roadster With Thrusters That Let It Hover and Turn in Mid-Air
stories.summary:
Tesla unveiled a new version of its Roadster electric sports car in Texas, equipped with thrusters that appear to allow it to hover and turn in mid-air. CEO Elon Musk presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.

"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk told the audience, saying a live crowd was needed to prove the demonstration "is not AI." The car was shown driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air and landing using air jets.

The BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman said there are several reasons a flying car is unlikely to appear on public roads anytime soon. The unveiling was covered by ABC News, BBC News and CBS News.

stories.headline: Update: Houthis Strike Aden Airport and Saudi Aramco Complex as Iran War Widens
stories.summary:
Yemen's Houthi rebels struck the main airport in the interim capital of Aden on Friday, while missiles and drones fired toward Saudi Arabia were intercepted, Bloomberg reported. The attack followed ballistic missile strikes on al-Maashiq Palace, after which Yemen's information minister said the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt. The Saudi energy ministry said a Houthi attack caused a "limited fire" at Aramco's headquarters complex in Dhahran.

The fighting is also reaching beyond Yemen's borders. A dozen people were killed Saturday in what Saudi aviation authorities called a "brutal" attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The Houthi missile strikes also threaten key supply routes on Yemen's Red Sea coast, intensifying pressure on government forces. BBC security correspondent Frank Gardner said the Iran-backed group's precision strikes and guerrilla tactics have made it hard for Saudi forces to gain the upper hand.

The escalation is tied to the wider war with Iran. Data from a monitoring agency shows attacks around the Strait of Hormuz at a record high, with two more vessels reporting attacks Friday, and all 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was struck by a projectile. Adm. Brad Cooper, the US Central Command commander, said Friday that the US naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in crude oil revenue. Experts say US military assistance and shuttle tankers and pipelines bypassing Hormuz have helped Gulf exports rebound. Analysts expect continued strikes on Saudi infrastructure, and no sign of de-escalation has emerged.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Denies Restricting Ukraine's Starlink Access as Reuters Cites White House Order
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump denied that he or Elon Musk limited Ukraine's access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to Starlink. "It wasn't me and I don't think it was Elon," he said, adding that he was "not sure" the network "ever came down." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier that normal speeds had not been restored.

Reuters reported Thursday, citing two unnamed US officials and a Western official, that the order came from inside the White House. Musk suggested the US government manages Starshield and that the Pentagon could have been responsible. On Tuesday night, speeds were reportedly capped at 100 mph, cutting off connectivity to faster weapons, and Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes that left about 600,000 people without power.

The dispute follows tension over a US-Russia diesel deal and Zelensky's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries, which Trump criticized. Washington had earlier warned it could withhold intelligence if the strikes continued. Trump said he has a good relationship with Zelensky, though he had earlier called him "more difficult to deal with" than Vladimir Putin. Zelensky told EU leaders on Friday, "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" while French President Emmanuel Macron pledged that EU states would not abandon Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators has demanded an investigation into the disruption, which they said degraded Ukraine's defensive operations.

stories.headline: Update: Midterm Fight Intensifies as Democrats Lead Polls and Fundraising, Justice Department Warns California Officials
stories.summary:
Less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, a national Times/Siena poll showed Democrats leading the congressional ballot by nearly nine percentage points. Democratic Senate candidates in more than a dozen competitive races raised a combined $253 million from July through September, more than four times the $56 million raised by Republicans in those races. Alaska is emerging as a pivotal contest, where Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola clashed in a debate over fuel costs tied to the war with Iran and allegations about Peltola's treatment of staff.

The Justice Department escalated its fight with California, warning in a letter that local officials who knowingly tabulate ballots cast by noncitizens could face criminal investigation and prosecution. Voting rights advocates fear the administration could use federal power to cast doubt on the election's results. Administration supporters say the actions are needed to enforce voter-roll requirements and keep noncitizens from voting.

Republicans face a difficult environment. Trump's approval stands near 37 percent, according to Silver Bulletin, and some conservatives are blaming Senate Majority Leader John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE America Act. Democrats are working to tie GOP opponents to Trump's economic policies and the Iran war. The House majority is thin, with Republicans holding 218 seats, and Cook rates 21 districts as toss-ups. Suspicious letters have also been sent to election offices and congressional offices, which federal investigators are examining.

stories.headline: Update: More Lawmakers Report Suspicious Mailings as Federal Investigators Probe Letters
stories.summary:
Several lawmakers said Friday that their offices across the country had received suspicious mailings. The reports follow earlier ones this week of letters containing unknown substances sent to US election offices. Among those affected are Sens. Amy Klobuchar, Tina Smith, Mike Rounds, Pete Ricketts and Ted Cruz, along with more than 15 House members.

Federal investigators said they are looking into the letters containing unknown substances mailed to state election officials and congressional offices. The incidents span both parties and several states. The substances have not been publicly identified in the reports provided.

The mailings come weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, adding security concerns for election administrators already dealing with legal disputes and heightened tension over ballot counting. Further details on the investigation's findings are expected.
